q: What is white tea and how is it made?
What are the different types of white tea?
What is Silver Needle (Bai Hao Yinzhen) tea?
What is White Peony (Bai Mu Dan) tea?
How is white tea different from green tea?
What does white tea taste like?
a: White tea is the least processed of all true teas, made from young, unopened tea buds and leaves that are simply withered and dried with minimal handling. The most prized white tea is Bai Hao Yinzhen (Silver Needle), made exclusively from unopened buds covered in fine white hairs, producing a pale, delicate liquor with a subtly sweet, floral flavor and a silky mouthfeel. Bai Mu Dan (White Peony) includes both buds and young leaves, resulting in a fuller body and more complex flavor than Silver Needle—it is the most popular white tea worldwide. Shou Mei and Gong Mei are made from more mature leaves and are often aged or pressed into cakes, developing deeper, earthier flavors over time. White tea contains the highest concentration of antioxidants among tea types due to minimal processing, and is traditionally from Fujian province in China.

q: What are the different types of green tea?
What is the difference between Chinese and Japanese green tea?
What is matcha and how is it different from regular green tea?
What are the different Japanese green tea varieties?
What is Dragon Well (Longjing) tea?
How is matcha made?
a: Green tea is unoxidized tea that is quickly heated after plucking to prevent oxidation—Chinese green teas are typically pan-fired (roasted in a wok), producing toasty, nutty flavors, while Japanese green teas are steamed, yielding grassy, vegetal, umami-rich flavors. Famous Chinese green teas include Dragon Well (Longjing) with its flat, sword-shaped leaves and chestnut flavor, Bi Luo Chun (Green Snail Spring) with tight spirals and fruity notes, and Gunpowder tea rolled into small pellets. Japanese green tea varieties include Sencha (the most common, steamed and rolled), Gyokuro (shade-grown for 20 days, highest umami), Matcha (shade-grown, stone-ground into a fine powder), Genmaicha (Sencha blended with roasted brown rice), Hojicha (roasted over charcoal, low caffeine), and Bancha (made from later harvest leaves). Matcha is uniquely shade-grown for 3-4 weeks before harvest to boost chlorophyll and L-theanine, then steamed, stemmed, deveined, and stone-ground into a vibrant green powder—ceremonial grade is used in Japanese tea ceremony, while culinary grade is used for lattes and cooking.

q: What is oolong tea?
How is oolong tea processed?
What are the main Chinese oolong teas?
What are the main Taiwanese oolong teas?
What is Tieguanyin (Iron Goddess) tea?
What is Da Hong Pao (Big Red Robe)?
What is the difference between Chinese and Taiwanese oolong?
a: Oolong tea is partially oxidized, ranging from 10% to 80% oxidation, placing it between green and black tea in flavor and appearance—this wide oxidation range produces an extraordinary variety of flavors from floral and creamy to woody and roasted. Chinese oolongs include Tieguanyin (Iron Goddess of Mercy) from Anxi, a light, floral, lingeringly sweet oolong; Da Hong Pao (Big Red Robe) from Wuyi Mountain, a dark, mineral-rich, heavily roasted rock tea; and Phoenix Dan Cong from Guangdong, known for its intense floral and fruity aromas (specific bushes produce distinct notes like honey orchid or almond). Taiwanese oolongs include Ali Shan and Dong Ding (both high-mountain, creamy, floral), Jin Xuan (known for a natural milky flavor), Si Ji Chun (Four Seasons, harvested year-round), Bao Zhong (lightly twisted, floral), and Oriental Beauty (Bai Hao Oolong), the most oxidized Taiwanese oolong, with white-tipped leaves and honey-fruity flavor. The key difference is that most Taiwanese oolongs are rolled into ball form, while Chinese oolongs range from tightly twisted strips (rock teas) to curled leaves (Tieguanyin).

q: What is black tea and how is it processed?
What are the different types of black tea?
What is the difference between Assam, Darjeeling, and Ceylon tea?
What is Earl Grey tea?
What is pu-erh tea?
What is the difference between sheng and shou pu-erh?
What are herbal teas (tisanes)?
a: Black tea is fully oxidized (100% oxidation), resulting in a dark, robust liquor with higher caffeine than other true teas—major black tea regions produce distinctly different flavor profiles. Assam (India) yields bold, malty, full-bodied teas; Darjeeling (India) produces delicate, muscatel-flavored teas with floral notes (first flush is light and floral, second flush is fruity with muscatel character); Ceylon (Sri Lanka) offers bright, citrusy, brisk teas; Keemun (China) is winey, fruity, and smooth; and Yunnan (China) produces earthy, peppery, sweet teas with a distinctive golden tip. Earl Grey is black tea flavored with bergamot oil, while English Breakfast is a robust blend of Assam, Ceylon, and Kenyan teas. Pu-erh is a post-fermented tea from Yunnan that undergoes microbial aging: sheng (raw) pu-erh is aged naturally for years or decades, developing complex, woody, fruity flavors; shou (ripe) pu-erh is pile-fermented (wo dui) to accelerate aging in months, producing dark, earthy, smooth, mushroom-like flavors. Herbal teas (tisanes) are not true tea (they contain no Camellia sinensis) and are caffeine-free—common tisanes include chamomile (calming), peppermint (digestive), rooibos (South African, naturally sweet), hibiscus (tart, high vitamin C), and ginger (warming, anti-inflammatory).
